extracted.intended_audience: general readers; law students; journalists; legal practitioners interested in U.S. defamation and First Amendment law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal standards and doctrinal tests established in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan and related cases for when plaintiffs (public officials/figures vs. private persons) may recover for alleged defamatory statements under the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual malice standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A public official (or candidate) suing for defamation must prove that the defendant made the statement with 'actual malice' — i.e., with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central constitutional requirement established by New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (376 U.S. 254 (1964)). The Court framed the rule as necessary to protect 'wide-open' debate about public issues; it substantially raises the plaintiff's burden and limits recovery for reputational harms when the plaintiff is a public official or public figure. Examples and subsequent case law show application and tests for reckless disregard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must prove falsity in public-official cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In defamation suits involving American public officials, the official-plaintiff bears the burden of proving that the defendant's statement was false (contrasting with older common-law approaches that placed the burden on the defendant to prove truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court held this shift is required by the First Amendment. The requirement was emphasized as one of two additional limitations (along with actual malice and the requirement that the statement concern the official individually).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamatory statement must concern the official individually, not general government policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A public official seeking damages must prove that the allegedly defamatory statement was about the official individually rather than being merely a critique of government policy or official actions generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation narrows recovery by distinguishing statements that target an individual's official conduct from broader criticisms of government institutions or policies, which are afforded greater protection under the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional protection for erroneous statements honestly made
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous statements are inevitable in free debate and, to preserve the 'breathing space' necessary for robust public discussion, the First Amendment must protect erroneous statements that are honestly made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court explicitly recognized that protecting some false statements is necessary to avoid chilling speech. This normative principle underlies the actual malice rule and counsels against strict liability for inaccuracies in public-issue speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of higher standard to public figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has extended Sullivan's higher actual-malice standard beyond public officials to cover 'public figures' — making it difficult for public figures to recover for defamation absent proof of actual malice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent decisions (and doctrine) treat public figures similarly to public officials for First Amendment purposes. The distinction between private persons, limited public figures, and all-purpose public figures affects the applicable standard and plaintiffs' burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standard for private persons (negligence-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: For private persons, the Court later held (e.g., Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., 418 U.S. 323 (1974)) that actual malice is not required; states may allow recovery upon a showing of at least negligence in publishing false statements about private individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gertz created a lower constitutional threshold for private plaintiffs, permitting states to set standards (often negligence) for defamatory falsehoods about private persons, while still protecting some speech interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: State procedural requirement for punitive damages (Alabama retraction-demand rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Alabama statute at issue, public officers were barred from recovering punitive damages for libel about official conduct unless they first made a written demand for a public retraction and the defendant failed or refused to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/state-law rule that factored into the case's background (Sullivan sent such a request; the Times did not publish a retraction). The Supreme Court's constitutional holding, however, is about First Amendment limits on liability irrespective of state procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of actual malice into related torts (false light, IIED)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court applied the Sullivan actual-malice framework in related privacy/defamation contexts — e.g., Time, Inc. v. Hill extended considerations to false-light invasion of privacy; Hustler Magazine v. Falwell applied First Amendment principles to intentional infliction of emotional distress claims involving public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These extensions illustrate that the actual-malice protection can limit recovery in torts beyond traditional libel when the claim implicates core First Amendment concerns about debate on public issues or public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited-public-figure test (thrusting into a public controversy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may be treated as a 'limited public figure' — and thus required to meet the higher standard — if they 'thrust themselves to the forefront of particular public controversies' and thereby invite attention and comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references application of this concept in later litigation (e.g., the McKee matter) where lower courts found a plaintiff to be a limited public figure for purposes of Sullivan, affecting the burden to show actual malice.
